etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hardshipe, equivalent to hard +‎ -ship.

quote.citation: 1962 December, “Dr. Beeching previews the plan for British Railways”, in Modern Railways, page 377:
quote.text: If train services of this kind were to be cut off, without any provision of alternative services, there would, of course, be hardship in some cases.

quote.citation: 2020 May 20, Philip Haigh, “Ribblehead: at the heart of the S&C's survival and its revival”, in Rail, page 26:
quote.text: The TUCC's role was to assess what (if any) hardship a BR closure proposal would cause, and to make recommendations to ministers who would have the final say.

definitions.definition: A burden, a source of difficulty that could impose a barrier.
(transitive) To treat (a person) badly; to subject to hardships.

quote.text: […]  an adjustment of the income tax could easily produce the twenty millions without hardshipping any industrious person in the community  […]

quote.citation: 1970, Reading Reform Foundation, The Annual Reading Reform Foundation Conference, page 47:
quote.text: Although we lost the election by the narrowest of margins, the people of Oregon heard a great deal about education, and particularly about how "look-say" reading instruction was hardshipping Oregon school children.
